findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG, EXTENSOR DIGITORUM COMMUNIS

Indication: Dysphagia and dysarthria; neuromuscular junction assessment

TECHNIQUE: Voluntary activation, concentric needle, 20 fibre pairs

RESULTS:
  Mean consecutive difference (MCD): 74 us [reference <34 us for age] ABNORMAL
  Fibre pairs with increased jitter: 15 of 20
  Blocking: 32% of fibre pairs

CONCLUSION: Markedly increased jitter with blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions: Pyridostigmine with levodopa-carbidopa: no pharmacokinetic interaction. Additive gastrointestinal effects (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea) are possible.
Pyridostigmine with amlodipine or aspirin: no clinically relevant interaction.
Anticholinergic antiparkinsonian drugs (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine), not on the current list, would antagonise the muscarinic effects of pyridostigmine.
Corticosteroids in older patients with Parkinson disease: risk of confusion, hyperglycaemia and blood pressure change; monitor.
warnings: Metoclopramide and other dopamine antagonists worsen parkinsonism; avoid.
Myasthenia gravis: avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium where possible; neuromuscular blockers need reduced doses with quantitative monitoring.
Levodopa must not be stopped abruptly (risk of parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome); give it by nasogastric tube if swallowing fails.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 4.2 nmol/L and blocking antibody 38%; MuSK not detected; normal thyroid function.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fluctuating dysphagia, dysarthria and nasal regurgitation out of proportion to mild Parkinson disease: AChR antibodies are the first test for late-onset bulbar MG (Jacob 2025; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 22% in orbicularis oculi, 19% in nasalis and 11% in trapezius without facilitation; no denervation on needle EMG including genioglossus.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation with needle EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms a postsynaptic transmission defect with cranial predominance, and the needle EMG of bulbar and limb muscles addresses bulbar-onset ALS (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lung cancer recurrence; fatty thymic involution without a mass; bronchiectasis and ground-glass change from recurrent aspiration.
action_criteria.label: Order CT of the chest and mediastinum with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG, and the same study answers the family's question about recurrence of the resected lung cancer and shows the aspiration damage.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 3.2 L (82% predicted, 48.5 mL/kg), MIP -62 cmH2O, MEP 96 cmH2O.
action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity and mouth pressures
action_criteria.rationale: Severe bulbar weakness with aspiration carries a risk of respiratory decompensation; a baseline makes later decline measurable.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in extensor digitorum communis.
action_criteria.label: Order single-fibre EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Not needed once RNS shows a decrement and AChR antibodies are positive; SFEMG does not separate MG from motor neuron disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pharmacokinetic interaction between pyridostigmine and levodopa-carbidopa; avoid dopamine antagonists.
action_criteria.label: Check pyridostigmine against his Parkinson medicines
action_criteria.rationale: No concrete interaction changes management; a reasonable check before starting pyridostigmine in a patient on levodopa.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on late-onset bulbar MG and its management.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on late-onset bulbar MG
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not prescribe metoclopramide for nausea or dysphagia: it worsens parkinsonism.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or Parkinson disease cause before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
required_recommendations: Admit for severe bulbar weakness with aspiration and weight loss, and give IVIG 2 g/kg over 2 to 5 days or plasma exchange.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily, 30 to 60 minutes before meals, titrated to effect (oral solution or via nasogastric tube if swallowing fails).

Start prednisolone at a low dose and titrate upward under inpatient monitoring, with glucose monitoring and bone protection; plan a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing) for long-term treatment.
Keep him nil by mouth for thin liquids pending a speech and language therapy swallow assessment; start nasogastric feeding and dietitian review for the 11 kg weight loss.
Monitor bulbar function, cough and respiratory function serially while weak; escalate if vital capacity or mouth pressures fall.
Continue levodopa-carbidopa without interruption (via nasogastric tube if needed) and coordinate with the Parkinson team.
Treat aspiration pneumonia, if it develops, with an MG-safe antibiotic (not a fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside or macrolide).

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure or episodic disturbance of consciousness; EEG does not inform bulbar weakness.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); nothing suggests meningeal or inflammatory CNS disease.
Contrast CT shows no lung cancer recurrence and the weight loss follows the dysphagia; FDG-PET has no place in the MG work-up.
No cardiac symptoms; the ECG shows only voltage LVH from hypertension.
Sinus rhythm, no palpitations or syncope; no arrhythmia question.

differential.key_features: Mild, stable parkinsonism for 4 years; Parkinson dysphagia is not fatigable and does not cause nasal regurgitation with palatal weakness, an RNS decrement or AChR antibodies.
No tongue wasting or fasciculations, no upper motor neuron signs, no denervation on needle EMG including genioglossus; decrement with AChR antibodies.

differential.diagnosis: Recurrent lung cancer with a paraneoplastic syndrome
differential.key_features: Adenocarcinoma resected 7 years ago; contrast CT shows no recurrence; weight loss follows the dysphagia.
Non-smoker with resected adenocarcinoma (not small cell); preserved reflexes, no autonomic features, normal baseline CMAPs without facilitation; AChR antibodies positive.
Fatigable bulbar weakness with a cranial RNS decrement and no long-tract or sensory signs.
Oropharyngeal dysphagia with nasal regurgitation, palatal and tongue weakness and dysarthria point to a neuromuscular cause, not an oesophageal one.

key_clinical_evidence: Two months of fluctuating dysphagia, hypophonic nasal speech and nasal regurgitation, worse at the end of meals and in the evening, with 11 kg weight loss, out of proportion to mild stable Parkinson disease.
Weak, asymmetric palatal elevation and weak tongue protrusion without wasting or fasciculations.
AChR binding 4.2 nmol/L and a 3 Hz decrement in facial and trapezius muscles without facilitation, with normal needle EMG: late-onset bulbar AChR-positive MG.
Contrast CT: no lung cancer recurrence, fatty thymic involution, and bronchiectasis with ground-glass change from recurrent aspiration.
Severe bulbar weakness with aspiration calls for IVIG or plasma exchange, nutrition by nasogastric tube and serial respiratory monitoring; thymectomy is not routine at 74 without thymoma.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: His parkinsonism is mild and stable; fatigable dysphagia with palatal weakness, a decrement and AChR antibodies establish MG.
red_herrings.data_point: Parkinson disease with hypophonia and masked face
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the dysphagia and dysarthria to Parkinson disease progression.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Contrast CT shows no recurrence; the weight loss follows the dysphagia, and the electrophysiology is postsynaptic without facilitation.
red_herrings.data_point: Lung adenocarcinoma resected 7 years ago, with weight loss
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue recurrence, a paraneoplastic syndrome or LEMS.

sequence_constraints.reason: Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).
AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Prior right upper lobe lung cancer; progressive dysphagia and weight loss

TECHNIQUE: Multi-detector CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm slices

FINDINGS:
LUNGS: Right upper lobe post-surgical changes with lobectomy defect. No new right upper lobe mass or consolidation. Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis and patchy peribronchial ground-glass opacities bilaterally, consistent with recurrent aspiration pneumonitis. No pleural effusion.

MEDIASTINUM: No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymus region: fatty involution (age-appropriate), no thymic mass.

BONES: No lytic or sclerotic lesions. No vertebral metastasis.

UPPER ABDOMEN: Normal liver, spleen, adrenal glands. No hepatic metastasis.

IMPRESSION:
1. No evidence of lung cancer recurrence or new malignancy.
2. Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis and peribronchial ground-glass opacities, consistent with recurrent aspiration.
3. No thymic mass or mediastinal adenopathy.

CONCLUSION: No evidence of malignancy or thoracic mass lesion. Bilateral lower lobe changes are consistent with recurrent aspiration. Clinical correlation recommended.

body_imaging.impression: 1. No evidence of lung cancer recurrence or new pulmonary mass; post-lobectomy changes. 2. Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis and patchy ground-glass opacities, consistent with recurrent aspiration. 3. Fatty involution of the thymus; no anterior mediastinal mass or lymphadenopathy.

AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. IVIG or plasma exchange is used for severe bulbar weakness and impending crisis.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: Late-onset MG (onset after 50) is increasingly recognised in older men; bulbar onset can be mistaken for stroke, motor neuron disease or other neurodegenerative disease.
results.source: Gilhus NE, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2570-2581

late-onset bulbar myasthenia gravis.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021) recommends AChR antibody testing first, electrodiagnostic confirmation, chest imaging for thymoma, and IVIG or plasma exchange for severe bulbar weakness. Late-onset MG is increasingly recognised in older men and bulbar onset can mimic other neurological disease (Gilhus 2016).

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive dysphagia and significant weight loss in a patient with Parkinson's disease and prior lung cancer

family_history: Father had Parkinson's disease; no family history of autoimmune or neuromuscular disease
past_medical_history: Right upper lobe lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma), resected 7 years ago; last CT 2 years ago showed no recurrence

patient.history_present_illness:
A 74-year-old Japanese man with a history of right upper lobe lung cancer resected 7 years ago (no evidence of recurrence at last follow-up 2 years prior) and Parkinson's disease diagnosed 4 years ago was admitted for progressive dysphagia and 11 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He described initial difficulty swallowing solid foods with bolus sticking in his throat, which progressed over several weeks to difficulty with pureed foods and liquids, causing frequent coughing and near-aspiration episodes. He also noted a muffled, hypophonic quality to his voice and nasal regurgitation of liquids on two occasions. Swallowing and speech were worse towards the end of meals and in the evening, and better after rest.

His Parkinson's disease was reasonably controlled; he still shuffled slightly on gait, had mild bilateral resting hand tremor, and occasional freezing episodes, but had been functionally independent in most ADLs until this dysphagia began. He was taking levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily. He had a fixed mild festinating gait attributed to Parkinson's disease for over 3 years without significant change.

The patient had no diplopia, ptosis, or limb weakness. He denied headache, fever, or night sweats. His family expressed concern about a possible cancer recurrence given the prior lung cancer history. On examination, he was moderately wasted (weight 66 kg, BMI 20.8, down from 77 kg two months earlier). Neurological assessment showed impaired pharyngeal reflex and failure on water-swallowing testing with pooling at the base of the tongue. Limb strength was 5/5 bilaterally. Balance was impaired (Berg Balance Scale 36). MMSE was 26. Mild festinating gait was confirmed.

A chest radiograph showed patchy bilateral lower-zone opacities. Admitting team initially attributed dysphagia to Parkinson's disease-related oropharyngeal dysfunction, but the severity was felt disproportionate to Parkinson's disease stage.

Impaired pharyngeal reflex; water swallowing test failed (coughing, pooling). Palate elevation: asymmetric and weak, left more than right. Tongue: weak voluntary protrusion, no wasting or fasciculations.
